newsitem.title: PERU: Five killed, 15 missing in southern Peru flooding.
newsitem.headline: Five killed, 15 missing in southern Peru flooding.

text.p: At least five people died and 15 others were missing on Wednesday in southern Peru when thunderstorms triggered severe flash-flooding in the Andean city of Arequipa, authorities said.
"Until midday, there were five dead. That figure is probably higher by now," a Civil Defence spokesman in Arequipa told Reuters.
Peruvian television put the death toll at seven.

He also said 15 people were missing while up to 1,500 families were homeless in poor and middle-class areas of Arequipa, Peru's second city located in Andean desert some 600 miles (1,000 kms) south of Lima.
"The flood was terrible. Houses are full of mud and rocks. Most heavily damnaged are extensive farming areas," said the spokesman, who asked not to named.
Among the dead were three children ages two, three and 14, including an infant who was dropped by her father when he was toppled by a rush of flooding water, he said.
The deaths followed a massive mudslide last week in the Apurimac region of Peru's southern Andes which obliterated two entire villages and killed up to 300 people.
Torrential weekend rains in the northern jungle region of Moyobamba flooded 1,000 houses and killed three people.
Continuing rains have prompted severe flooding in Peru's northern Amazon, leaving another 600 families isolated, local radio reported.
A scientist said deforestation and erosion in Peru's north have left village dwellers more exposed then ever to disaster.
Meteorologist Felix Cubas said that irresponsible forest management had left the people of northern Peru at an increased risk of flooding during the January-March rainy season.
"These days, deforestation means there is no defence against erosion and rivers breaking their banks," he said.
President Alberto Fujimori, visiting severely flooded areas in the southern Andean altiplano region of Puno, handed out blankets and other supplies Wednesday to scores of homeless families.
"Everything is affected," a flood victim told local television. "It looks like this year we are not going to get anything for our harvets."
Another said floods had left his community dangerously exposed. "Right now, we're susceptible to diseases and the cold," he said.
